summary: Psalm 21 begins with the king rejoicing because Yahweh has answered his desires, given him life, crowned him, and made him glad in God's presence. The poem then turns from the king's blessing to the defeat of enemies and their evil plans. It ends by asking Yahweh to be exalted in strength so the people can sing and praise his power.
whyItMatters: This psalm shows royal praise from inside Book I of Psalms: the king's security is not presented as self-made, but as grounded in Yahweh's strength, salvation, and loving kindness. It also introduces the harder royal theme of divine judgment against enemies without explaining every historical circumstance behind the conflict.

context.author: The heading says, “A Psalm by David.” Davidic headings are ancient features of the collection, but readers differ on whether each one means authorship, association, dedication, or belonging to a Davidic collection.
context.audience: Israel's worshiping and instructed community, with later Jewish and Christian communities also receiving the Psalms as prayer and Scripture.
context.date: Individual psalms may preserve material from the monarchy through the postexilic period; a precise date for Psalm 21 cannot be established from its wording and heading alone.
context.setting: A royal psalm in the Hebrew Psalter's Book I, where David-associated prayers of distress and confidence are prominent.
context.literaryForm: Compressed Hebrew poetry and prayer, shaped by praise, parallel lines, royal imagery, and a closing communal call to sing.

outline.heading: The king rejoices
outline.note: The poem opens with the king rejoicing in Yahweh's strength and salvation because his request has not been withheld.

outline.heading: Blessing and crown
outline.note: Yahweh is praised for meeting the king with goodness, setting a crown on him, giving life, and placing honor, majesty, blessing, and joy on him.

outline.heading: Trust and stability
outline.note: The king's security is tied to trust in Yahweh and to the loving kindness of the Most High.

outline.heading: Enemies found and judged
outline.note: The poem turns to hostile enemies and their failed plots, describing defeat through divine wrath, fire, and aimed bows.

outline.heading: Final praise
outline.note: The congregation asks Yahweh to be exalted in strength and promises song and praise.

keyVerses.text: For the Chief Musician. A Psalm by David. The king rejoices in your strength, Yahweh! How greatly he rejoices in your salvation!
keyVerses.why: This verse states the chapter's opening mood and its main source of confidence: the king rejoices because of Yahweh's strength and salvation.

keyVerses.text: He asked life of you and you gave it to him, even length of days forever and ever.
keyVerses.why: This verse anchors the poem's royal blessing language by naming life and enduring days as gifts from God.

keyVerses.text: For the king trusts in Yahweh. Through the loving kindness of the Most High, he shall not be moved.
keyVerses.why: This verse explains the king's stability as trust in Yahweh and dependence on divine loving kindness.

keyVerses.text: Be exalted, Yahweh, in your strength, so we will sing and praise your power.
keyVerses.why: The final verse turns the poem into communal praise, ending where it began: Yahweh's strength.

themes: life and blessing given to the king
judgment on enemies who plot evil

questions.question: Who is “the king” in this psalm?
questions.answer: The chapter itself calls the central figure “the king” and presents him as someone who rejoices in Yahweh's strength, receives a crown, and trusts in Yahweh. The heading associates the psalm with David, but readers differ on how Davidic headings should be understood. So the safest reading begins with the poem's royal figure, while recognizing its Davidic association in the received Psalter.

questions.question: What does “Selah” mean here?
questions.answer: “Selah” appears at the end of verse 2. It is an uncertain musical or performance marker, often preserved because its exact instruction is no longer known. Here it likely marks some kind of pause or performance signal, but its exact function remains uncertain.

questions.question: What request has Yahweh answered?
questions.answer: Verse 2 says Yahweh gave the king his heart's desire and did not withhold the request of his lips. Verse 4 names one request directly: “He asked life of you and you gave it to him.” The chapter does not describe the original situation in detail, so the answer should stay with those stated gifts.

questions.question: Is the crown in verse 3 literal or symbolic?
questions.answer: The verse says, “You set a crown of fine gold on his head,” which fits the psalm's royal setting. Readers may understand it as referring to actual royal honor, poetic imagery for Yahweh's favor, or both. The chapter does not explain a particular coronation scene, so it is best not to build one from the line alone.

questions.question: Does “forever and ever” mean the king personally never dies?
questions.answer: Verse 4 says Yahweh gave the king “length of days forever and ever,” and verse 6 also says Yahweh makes him “most blessed forever.” Readers differ on how royal psalms speak about enduring kingship: some hear ideal royal language, some connect it with the Davidic line, and later Jewish and Christian readers may hear messianic hope. The chapter itself emphasizes that lasting life and blessing come from Yahweh, without spelling out all later applications.

questions.question: What keeps the king from being “moved”?
questions.answer: Verse 7 gives two reasons: the king trusts in Yahweh, and he is held through the loving kindness of the Most High. The psalm does not portray the king as secure because of military skill or personal greatness. His stability is described as dependence on God.

questions.question: Why does the psalm speak so fiercely about enemies?
questions.answer: Verses 8-12 describe enemies who hate and plot against the one being addressed. The shift between “you” and “Yahweh” in verse 9 leaves room to read the king’s battle and God’s judgment together rather than assigning every address to one figure. The language is severe: fire, wrath, destroyed descendants, and drawn bows. It presents royal victory and divine judgment, without authorizing private revenge.

questions.question: Who is singing at the end?
questions.answer: Verse 13 shifts to “we,” saying, “so we will sing and praise your power.” That sounds like a communal voice answering the royal praise and judgment language that came before. The chapter ends not with the king's achievement, but with worship directed to Yahweh's strength and power.
